title: Electric fields and capacitors
subtitle: Coulomb's law, field strength, potential, capacitance, energy and discharge

types.name: Coulomb's law between two point charges
types.method: Use Coulomb's law whenever two point charges (or charged spheres, ions, nuclei, electrons) are a known distance apart. Convert every charge to coulombs and every distance to metres before substituting, then square the separation. The sign tells you attract or repel; the question usually wants the magnitude.
commonErrors: Forgetting to square r, or squaring the prefix wrongly (3.0 mm → 9.0 × 10⁻⁶ m², not 9.0 × 10⁻³)
Entering 1 / (4πε₀) as 4π × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² instead of 1 / (4π × 8.85 × 10⁻¹²) = 8.99 × 10⁹
Dividing a charge in nC by 10⁹ instead of multiplying by 10⁻⁹ and losing the power of ten

worked.question: Two small charged spheres in a laboratory carry charges of +3.0 μC and +5.0 μC. Their centres are 0.20 m apart. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them.
steps: Known: Q = 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ C, q = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ C, r = 0.20 m. Unknown: F.
F = Qq / (4πε₀r²), with 1 / (4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²
F = 3.37 N (repulsive, since both charges are positive)

practice.question: A charged balloon carrying +40 nC is held 0.15 m from a small metal sphere carrying −25 nC. Calculate the magnitude of the force between them.
practice.hint: Convert both charges to coulombs (1 nC = 10⁻⁹ C) and substitute into F = Qq / (4πε₀r²); ignore the signs for the magnitude.

practice.question: In a hydrogen atom the electron is, on average, 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m from the proton. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them.
practice.hint: Both charges have magnitude e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; substitute into F = Qq / (4πε₀r²).

practice.question: Two toner particles in a photocopier each carry a charge of 2.0 nC and are 3.0 mm apart. Calculate the electrostatic force between them.
practice.hint: Convert 3.0 mm to metres before squaring it.

practice.question: In a crystal of sodium chloride, a Na⁺ ion and a neighbouring Cl⁻ ion are 282 pm apart. Treating the ions as point charges, calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them.
practice.hint: Each ion carries a charge of magnitude e; 1 pm = 10⁻¹² m.

practice.question: Two identical polystyrene spheres are each given 2.5 × 10¹⁰ excess electrons and placed with their centres 8.0 cm apart. Calculate the repulsive force between them.
practice.hint: First find the charge on each sphere from Q = ne, then use Coulomb's law with r in metres.
walkthrough: Q = ne = 2.5 × 10¹⁰ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ C on each sphere

practice.question: In a scattering experiment an alpha particle (charge +2e) approaches a gold nucleus (charge +79e). Calculate the separation at which the repulsive force between them is 2.0 N.
practice.hint: Work out both charges as multiples of e, then rearrange F = Qq / (4πε₀r²) for r and remember the square root.

types.name: Electric field strength of a point charge
types.method: Field strength is the force per unit positive charge. For a radial field around a point charge use E = Q / (4πε₀r²) with Q the charge producing the field and r the distance from its centre. If you are given a force on a known test charge, use E = F / Q instead. Rearranging for r needs a square root.
commonErrors: Using the test charge instead of the source charge in E = Q / (4πε₀r²)
Forgetting the square root when rearranging for r
Writing the unit as N or V instead of N C⁻¹ (equivalently V m⁻¹)

worked.question: A Van de Graaff dome carries a charge of +2.0 μC. Treating the dome as a point charge, calculate the electric field strength at a point 0.30 m from its centre.
steps: Known: Q = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C, r = 0.30 m. Unknown: E.
E = Q / (4πε₀r²), with 1 / (4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²

practice.question: A small charged sphere carries +60 nC. Calculate the electric field strength at a point 1.2 m from its centre.
practice.hint: Convert 60 nC to coulombs and substitute into E = Q / (4πε₀r²).

practice.question: A test charge of +4.0 nC placed in an electric field experiences a force of 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ N. Calculate the electric field strength at that point.
practice.hint: Field strength is force per unit charge: E = F / Q.

practice.question: Calculate the electric field strength at a distance of 1.0 nm from a proton.
practice.hint: The proton's charge is e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; convert 1.0 nm to metres before squaring.

practice.question: The electric field strength 0.20 m from the centre of a charged sphere is 5.0 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. Calculate the charge on the sphere, in nC.
practice.hint: Rearrange E = Q / (4πε₀r²) to give Q = 4πε₀Er², then divide by 10⁻⁹ to convert to nC.

practice.question: Air breaks down (sparks) when the electric field strength reaches 3.0 × 10⁶ N C⁻¹. Calculate the distance from the centre of a point charge of +8.0 μC at which the field strength has this value.
practice.hint: Rearrange E = Q / (4πε₀r²) for r² and take the square root.

practice.question: A charged pith ball carries +3.0 μC. A second ball carrying −20 nC is placed 0.25 m from its centre. By first finding the electric field strength due to the first ball at the second ball, calculate the magnitude of the force on the second ball.
practice.hint: Find E from the +3.0 μC charge using E = Q / (4πε₀r²), then use F = EQ with the −20 nC charge.

types.name: Uniform field between parallel plates
types.method: Between two parallel plates the field is uniform: E = V / d, where V is the p.d. between the plates and d their separation in metres. A charge Q in the field feels a constant force F = EQ, so a particle of mass m accelerates at a = EQ / m. Convert mm or cm to metres and kV to volts first.
commonErrors: Leaving the plate separation in mm or cm
Using the electron charge without the mass (or the proton mass for an electron) when finding acceleration
Writing E = Vd instead of V / d

worked.question: Two parallel metal plates 4.0 cm apart have a p.d. of 2.0 kV across them. Calculate the force on a dust particle carrying a charge of +3.0 nC that is between the plates.
steps: Known: V = 2000 V, d = 0.040 m, Q = 3.0 × 10⁻⁹ C. Unknown: F.
First the field strength: E = V / d = 2000 / 0.040 = 5.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹

practice.question: The deflecting plates in an oscilloscope are 0.050 m apart and have a p.d. of 600 V across them. Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.
practice.hint: The field between parallel plates is E = V / d.

practice.question: A charged oil drop carrying +8.0 nC sits in a uniform field of strength 2.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. Calculate the electric force on the drop.
practice.hint: Force on a charge in a field: F = EQ, with Q in coulombs.

practice.question: The plates of an electrostatic air filter are 8.0 mm apart and have 1500 V across them. Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.
practice.hint: Convert 8.0 mm to metres before dividing.

practice.question: A uniform field of strength 3.2 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ exists between two parallel plates 5.0 mm apart. Calculate the p.d. between the plates.
practice.hint: Rearrange E = V / d to V = Ed, with d in metres.

practice.question: In an electron gun, electrons are accelerated between two plates 20 mm apart with a p.d. of 250 V between them. Calculate the acceleration of an electron between the plates.
practice.hint: Find E = V / d, then the force F = eE, then a = F / m_e.

practice.question: In a mass spectrometer, singly charged argon ions (mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) are accelerated between two plates 3.0 cm apart with a p.d. of 1.2 kV. Calculate the acceleration of an ion between the plates.
practice.hint: A singly charged ion has charge e; find E = V / d, then a = eE / m.

types.name: Electric potential and potential energy
types.method: Potential at a distance r from a point charge is V = Q / (4πε₀r) — note r, not r². The potential energy of two point charges is E_p = Qq / (4πε₀r). Work done moving a charge q between two points is W = qΔV, so for a radial field find V at each point first and subtract.
commonErrors: Squaring r in the potential equation (that is the field strength equation)
Using only the final potential instead of the change ΔV when finding work done
Forgetting to convert an energy in joules to eV or MeV when the question asks for it

worked.question: A charged sphere carries +4.0 μC. Calculate the electric potential at a point 0.50 m from its centre.
steps: Known: Q = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ C, r = 0.50 m. Unknown: V.
V = Q / (4πε₀r), with 1 / (4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²

practice.question: A small sphere on a plastic rod carries +25 nC. Calculate the electric potential at a point 0.10 m from its centre.
practice.hint: V = Q / (4πε₀r) with Q in coulombs; no square on r.

practice.question: A charge of +3.0 μC is moved between two points in an electric field whose potentials differ by 250 V. Calculate the work done on the charge.
practice.hint: Work done = charge × potential difference, W = QΔV.

practice.question: In a hydrogen atom the electron and proton are 53 pm apart. Calculate the magnitude of the electric potential energy of the pair, in joules.
practice.hint: Use E_p = Qq / (4πε₀r) with both charges equal to e and r converted from pm to metres.

practice.question: The potential at a point near the dome of a Van de Graaff generator carrying +5.0 μC is 90 kV. Treating the dome as a point charge, calculate the distance of the point from the centre of the dome.
practice.hint: Rearrange V = Q / (4πε₀r) to give r = Q / (4πε₀V); convert kV to V.

practice.question: A charge of +2.0 nC is moved from a point 0.20 m from a +6.0 μC point charge to a point 0.50 m from it. Calculate the magnitude of the work done.
practice.hint: Find the potential at each distance using V = Q / (4πε₀r), subtract to get ΔV, then W = qΔV.

practice.question: An alpha particle (charge +2e) reaches a distance of 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m from the centre of a gold nucleus (charge +79e). Calculate the electric potential energy of the pair at this separation, in MeV.
practice.hint: Use E_p = Qq / (4πε₀r) with Q = 2e and q = 79e to get joules, then divide by 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J per MeV.

types.name: Capacitance, charge and p.d. (C = Q / V)
types.method: Capacitance is the charge stored per volt: C = Q / V. Identify which two of C, Q and V you have, convert prefixes (μF = 10⁻⁶ F, nF = 10⁻⁹ F, pF = 10⁻¹² F, mC = 10⁻³ C) and rearrange. If the charge comes from a constant current, find it first with Q = It.
commonErrors: Treating μF as 10⁻³ F or nF as 10⁻⁶ F
Giving the answer in F when the question asks for μF or nF (or the reverse)
Rearranging C = Q / V as Q = C / V instead of Q = CV

worked.question: A 220 μF smoothing capacitor in a power supply is charged to 10.0 V. Calculate the charge stored on it.
steps: Known: C = 220 × 10⁻⁶ F, V = 10.0 V. Unknown: Q.
C = Q / V, so Q = CV

practice.question: A capacitor stores 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ C of charge when the p.d. across it is 6.0 V. Calculate its capacitance in farads.
practice.hint: Capacitance is charge per volt: C = Q / V.

practice.question: A 100 μF capacitor in a camera flash unit carries a charge of 1.5 × 10⁻³ C. Calculate the p.d. across it.
practice.hint: Rearrange C = Q / V to V = Q / C, with C in farads.

practice.question: A 4700 μF capacitor in a car audio amplifier is charged to 25 V. Calculate the charge stored, in mC.
practice.hint: Q = CV gives coulombs; divide by 10⁻³ to convert to mC.

practice.question: A capacitor in a radio circuit stores 36 nC when charged to 12 V. Calculate its capacitance in nF.
practice.hint: C = Q / V; keeping Q in nC gives C directly in nF, or convert to coulombs and back.

practice.question: A capacitor is charged by a constant current of 50 μA for 40 s, after which the p.d. across it is 8.0 V. Calculate its capacitance in μF.
practice.hint: First find the charge from Q = It, then use C = Q / V.

practice.question: A 12 pF capacitor in a mobile phone circuit is charged to 5.0 V. Calculate the number of excess electrons on its negative plate.
practice.hint: Find the charge from Q = CV, then divide by e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

types.name: Parallel-plate capacitor (C = ε₀ε_rA / d)
types.method: The capacitance of two parallel plates depends on their overlap area A (in m²), separation d (in m) and the relative permittivity ε_r of what is between them (1 for air or vacuum). Convert cm² to m² (× 10⁻⁴) and mm to m (× 10⁻³) before substituting. Rearrange for d or ε_r by cross-multiplying.
commonErrors: Converting cm² to m² with 10⁻² instead of 10⁻⁴
Leaving out ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ and getting an answer of farads rather than picofarads
Putting d on top: C is inversely proportional to the separation

worked.question: Two parallel metal plates in a laboratory each have an area of 0.040 m² and are separated by 0.50 mm of air. Calculate the capacitance of the arrangement.
steps: Known: A = 0.040 m², d = 0.50 × 10⁻³ m, ε_r = 1 (air). Unknown: C.

practice.question: A simple air-spaced capacitor has plates of area 0.020 m² separated by 1.0 × 10⁻³ m. Calculate its capacitance.
practice.hint: For air, ε_r = 1, so C = ε₀A / d.

practice.question: A capacitor is made from two foil sheets of area 0.015 m² separated by a 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m layer of mica with relative permittivity 4.0. Calculate its capacitance.
practice.hint: Substitute directly into C = ε₀ε_rA / d, remembering to include ε_r.

practice.question: A capacitor in a tuning circuit has plates of area 25 cm² separated by 0.20 mm of polythene (ε_r = 2.3). Calculate its capacitance in pF.
practice.hint: Convert 25 cm² to m² (× 10⁻⁴) and 0.20 mm to m, then divide the answer in F by 10⁻¹².

practice.question: An air-spaced capacitor is to have a capacitance of 100 pF using plates of area 60 cm². Calculate the required plate separation in mm.
practice.hint: Rearrange C = ε₀A / d to d = ε₀A / C; convert cm² to m² and the answer from m to mm.

practice.question: A 4.7 nF capacitor has plates of area 0.012 m² separated by a 0.10 mm layer of dielectric. Calculate the relative permittivity of the dielectric.
practice.hint: Rearrange C = ε₀ε_rA / d to ε_r = Cd / (ε₀A).

practice.question: A capacitor has square plates of side 8.0 cm separated by 0.50 mm of ceramic with relative permittivity 6.0. It is connected to a 50 V supply. Calculate the charge stored.
practice.hint: Find A in m² and then C from C = ε₀ε_rA / d; then use Q = CV.

types.name: Energy stored in a capacitor
types.method: Choose the form of the energy equation that uses the two quantities you are given: ½QV, ½CV² or Q² / 2C. Energy delivered as the p.d. falls from V₁ to V₂ is ½C(V₁² − V₂²), so find the energy at each p.d. and subtract. To find V from energy, rearrange ½CV² and take the square root.
commonErrors: Forgetting the ½
Subtracting the p.d.s before squaring when finding energy delivered: use V₁² − V₂², not (V₁ − V₂)²
Forgetting the square root when rearranging for V

worked.question: A 2200 μF capacitor in a power supply is charged to 15 V. Calculate the energy stored.
steps: Known: C = 2200 × 10⁻⁶ F, V = 15 V. Unknown: E.
The two given quantities are C and V, so use E = ½CV²

practice.question: A capacitor holds 5.0 mC of charge at a p.d. of 20 V. Calculate the energy stored.
practice.hint: You have Q and V, so use E = ½QV with Q in coulombs.

practice.question: A 100 μF capacitor in a bicycle light is charged to 50 V. Calculate the energy stored.
practice.hint: Use E = ½CV² with C in farads.

practice.question: A 40 μF capacitor stores a charge of 0.60 mC. Calculate the energy stored.
practice.hint: You have Q and C, so use E = Q² / 2C after converting both prefixes.

practice.question: A defibrillator stores 200 J of energy in a 32 μF capacitor. Calculate the p.d. to which the capacitor is charged.
practice.hint: Rearrange E = ½CV² to V = √(2E / C).

practice.question: A 4700 μF capacitor charged to 12 V is used to power a small motor. The p.d. across the capacitor falls to 4.0 V. Calculate the energy delivered to the motor.
practice.hint: Find the stored energy at 12 V and at 4.0 V using ½CV², then subtract.

practice.question: A 1200 μF capacitor charged to 300 V discharges fully through a flash tube in 2.0 ms. Calculate the mean power delivered to the tube, in kW.
practice.hint: Find the stored energy with ½CV², then divide by the time in seconds.

types.name: Capacitors in series and parallel
types.method: Capacitors add directly in parallel and by reciprocals in series — the opposite way round to resistors. Work through a network one block at a time, replacing each parallel or series pair with its single equivalent. Capacitors in series all carry the same charge; capacitors in parallel all have the same p.d.
commonErrors: Using the resistor rules (adding in series, reciprocals in parallel)
Forgetting to take the reciprocal at the end of a series calculation
Mixing pF and nF in the same sum without converting

worked.question: A 2.0 μF capacitor and a 3.0 μF capacitor are connected in series. Calculate the combined capacitance.
steps: Known: C₁ = 2.0 μF, C₂ = 3.0 μF in series. Unknown: combined C.

practice.question: A 4.7 μF capacitor and a 10 μF capacitor are connected in parallel across a loudspeaker crossover. Calculate the combined capacitance.
practice.hint: Capacitors in parallel simply add.
walkthrough: C₁ = 4.7 μF, C₂ = 10 μF in parallel

practice.question: A 6.0 μF capacitor is connected in series with a 12 μF capacitor. Calculate the combined capacitance.
practice.hint: Use 1 / C = 1 / C₁ + 1 / C₂ and remember to invert at the end.

practice.question: In a radio tuning circuit a 2200 pF capacitor is connected in parallel with a 4.7 nF capacitor. Calculate the combined capacitance in nF.
practice.hint: Convert 2200 pF to nF (1 nF = 1000 pF) before adding.

practice.question: A capacitor of unknown capacitance is connected in series with a 10 μF capacitor. The combined capacitance is 4.0 μF. Calculate the unknown capacitance.
practice.hint: Rearrange the series rule: 1 / C₂ = 1 / C − 1 / C₁.

practice.question: A 2.0 μF capacitor and a 4.0 μF capacitor are connected in parallel, and this combination is connected in series with a 3.0 μF capacitor. Calculate the total capacitance of the network.
practice.hint: Combine the parallel pair first by adding, then treat the result as a single capacitor in series with the 3.0 μF.

practice.question: A 3.0 μF capacitor and a 6.0 μF capacitor are connected in series across an 18 V supply. Calculate the charge stored on the 3.0 μF capacitor, in μC.
practice.hint: Find the combined capacitance first; capacitors in series all carry the same charge, Q = C_total × V.
walkthrough: Series capacitors carry equal charge: Q = CV = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 18

types.name: Capacitor discharge through a resistor
types.method: Find the time constant τ = RC first (ohms × farads gives seconds). Then V, Q and I all fall as e^(−t/τ). To find a value after time t, evaluate the exponential. To find a time, divide by the starting value to get the fraction remaining, take the natural log of both sides and multiply by −τ.
commonErrors: Calculating RC with the capacitance in μF instead of F, giving a time constant 10⁶ too big
Taking log₁₀ instead of ln when solving for t
Dropping the minus sign: t = −RC ln(V / V₀), and ln of a fraction is negative so t comes out positive

worked.question: A 470 μF capacitor charged to 9.0 V discharges through a 10 kΩ resistor. Calculate the p.d. across the capacitor 6.0 s after the discharge begins.
steps: Known: V₀ = 9.0 V, R = 10 × 10³ Ω, C = 470 × 10⁻⁶ F, t = 6.0 s. Unknown: V.

practice.question: A 2200 μF capacitor discharges through a 1.5 kΩ resistor. Calculate the time constant of the circuit.
practice.hint: τ = RC with R in ohms and C in farads.

practice.question: A capacitor charged to 12 V discharges through a resistor in a circuit with a time constant of 5.0 s. Calculate the p.d. across the capacitor after 8.0 s.
practice.hint: Substitute directly into V = V₀e^(−t/τ).

practice.question: A 100 μF capacitor discharges through a 47 kΩ resistor. The initial current is 2.0 mA. Calculate the current after 10 s, in μA.
practice.hint: Find τ = RC, use I = I₀e^(−t/RC), then convert the answer from A to μA.

practice.question: A timing circuit uses a 50 μF capacitor and needs a time constant of 0.25 s. Calculate the resistance required, in kΩ.
practice.hint: Rearrange τ = RC to R = τ / C, then convert ohms to kΩ.

practice.question: A 330 μF capacitor discharges through a 22 kΩ resistor. Calculate the time taken for the p.d. across the capacitor to fall to 25% of its initial value.
practice.hint: Find τ = RC, then set V / V₀ = 0.25 and solve t = −RC ln(0.25).

practice.question: A capacitor discharges through a 100 kΩ resistor. The p.d. across it halves in 14 s. Calculate the capacitance, in μF.
practice.hint: Use V / V₀ = 0.5 = e^(−t/RC) to find RC first, then divide by R.

types.name: Capacitor charging through a resistor
types.method: When a capacitor charges through a resistor from a supply V₀, the p.d. across it rises as V = V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)). Find τ = RC first. To find a time, divide by V₀ to get the fraction reached, rearrange to e^(−t/RC) = 1 − fraction, then take ln and multiply by −RC.
commonErrors: Using the discharge equation V₀e^(−t/RC), which gives the p.d. across the resistor, not the capacitor
Taking ln of the fraction reached instead of ln of (1 − fraction)
Leaving C in μF or nF when calculating RC

worked.question: A 22 μF capacitor is charged from a 6.0 V supply through a 100 kΩ resistor. Calculate the p.d. across the capacitor 3.0 s after the switch is closed.
steps: Known: V₀ = 6.0 V, R = 100 × 10³ Ω, C = 22 × 10⁻⁶ F, t = 3.0 s. Unknown: V.

practice.question: A capacitor is charged from a 10 V supply through a resistor; the circuit's time constant is 4.0 s. Calculate the p.d. across the capacitor 2.0 s after charging begins.
practice.hint: Substitute directly into V = V₀(1 − e^(−t/τ)).

practice.question: A 1000 μF capacitor in a camera is charged from a 12 V battery through a 4.7 kΩ resistor. Calculate the p.d. across the capacitor 5.0 s after charging begins.
practice.hint: Find τ = RC first, then use V = V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)).

practice.question: A 470 nF capacitor is charged from a 5.0 V logic supply through a 2.2 MΩ resistor. Calculate the p.d. across the capacitor after 0.50 s.
practice.hint: Convert MΩ to Ω and nF to F before finding RC.

practice.question: A capacitor is charged from a 5.0 V supply in a circuit with a time constant of 3.0 s. Calculate the time taken for the p.d. across it to reach 2.0 V.
A 220 μF capacitor is charged through a 56 kΩ resistor. Calculate the time taken for the p.d. across the capacitor to reach 90% of the supply p.d.
practice.hint: Find τ = RC, then e^(−t/RC) = 1 − 0.90 = 0.10 and t = −RC ln(0.10).

practice.question: A 100 μF capacitor is charged through a resistor from a fixed supply. The p.d. across the capacitor reaches half the supply p.d. after 0.20 s. Calculate the resistance, in kΩ.
practice.hint: Use 0.5 = 1 − e^(−t/RC) to find RC first, then R = RC / C.

types.name: Reading field, potential and capacitor graphs
equations: E = −ΔV / Δr (gradient of a V–r graph; tangent on a curve)
ΔV = area under an E–r graph
W = ½QV = area under a V–Q graph
C = Q / V = gradient of a Q–V graph
V = V₀e^(−t/RC): V = 0.37 V₀ when t = RC
ln V = ln V₀ − t / RC (gradient = −1 / RC)
I = −ΔQ / Δt (gradient of a Q–t graph)
types.method: Decide what the gradient and the area of the graph mean before reading anything. Potential against distance: the gradient (of a tangent, on a curve) gives the field strength. Field strength against distance: the area gives the p.d. For a capacitor, the area under a V–Q graph is the energy stored and the gradient of a Q–V graph is the capacitance. On discharge curves the time constant RC is the time for V or Q to fall to 0.37 of its starting value, the tangent at t = 0 has gradient −Q₀ / RC, and ln V against t is a straight line of gradient −1 / RC. Convert axis scales (cm, μC, kV m⁻¹) to SI before quoting the answer.
commonErrors: Reading a gradient in V cm⁻¹ and forgetting to convert it to V m⁻¹
Using the whole area under a V–Q graph instead of the triangle up to the final charge, or forgetting the ½
Taking the time constant as the time for V to fall to half of V₀ (that is 0.69 RC, not RC)
Quoting the gradient of ln V against t as RC instead of −1 / RC

worked.question: The graph shows how the electric potential V varies with distance r from the centre of a charged metal sphere of radius 2.0 cm. The tangent to the curve at X is drawn. Use the graph to determine the magnitude of the electric field strength at X.
steps: Field strength is the potential gradient: E = −ΔV / Δr, so E at X is the gradient of the tangent at X.
The tangent passes through (1.0 cm, 2000 V) and (6.0 cm, 0 V).
Convert: 1 cm = 0.010 m, so gradient = −400 / 0.010 = −4.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹
E = 4.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ (magnitude; the field points outwards, down the potential slope)

graph.alt: Potential against distance from a charged sphere, falling as 1 over r from 1800 V at 2 cm to 360 V at 10 cm, with the tangent at X (3 cm, 1200 V) drawn from (1 cm, 2000 V) to (6 cm, 0)

practice.question: The graph shows how the charge Q stored on a capacitor varies with the p.d. V across it. Point X is marked on the line. Use the graph to determine the capacitance of the capacitor in μF.
practice.hint: C = Q / V, so the gradient of a Q–V line through the origin is the capacitance; the charge axis is in mC.
walkthrough: The line passes through the origin and X at (10 V, 1.5 mC).

graph.alt: Straight line through the origin of charge in mC against p.d., with point X marked at 10 V and 1.5 mC

practice.question: The graph shows how the p.d. V across a capacitor in a camera flash unit varies with the charge Q stored on it. Use the shaded area to determine the energy stored in the capacitor when it holds the charge at point P. Give your answer in J.
practice.hint: The energy stored is the area under the V–Q line, which is a triangle: ½ × base × height, with the charge converted from μC to C.
walkthrough: At P: Q = 50 μC = 50 × 10⁻⁶ C and V = 10 V.
Energy stored = area of the shaded triangle = ½ × Q × V

graph.alt: Straight line through the origin of p.d. against charge in μC, with the triangle under the line up to P (50 μC, 10 V) shaded

practice.question: The graph shows how the electric field strength E varies with distance r from the centre of the charged dome of a Van de Graaff generator. The area under the curve between A (r = 0.20 m) and B (r = 0.40 m) is shaded and contains 4.5 large squares. Use the graph to determine the potential difference between A and B.
practice.hint: The area under an E–r graph is the p.d.; work out what one large square represents from the axis scales, remembering the E axis is in kV m⁻¹.
walkthrough: P.d. = area under the E–r graph between A and B.
One large square is 0.05 m wide and 1 kV m⁻¹ = 1000 V m⁻¹ tall, so it represents 0.05 × 1000 = 50 V.

graph.alt: Field strength in kV per metre against distance from a charged dome, falling as 1 over r squared from 9 kV per metre at 0.10 m, with the area between r = 0.20 m and r = 0.40 m shaded

practice.question: A 2.7 V supercapacitor discharges through a resistor. The graph shows how the p.d. V across it varies with time t. Point X is marked where the p.d. has fallen to 0.37 of its initial value. Use the graph to determine the time constant of the circuit.
practice.hint: After one time constant the p.d. has fallen to V₀ / e = 0.37 V₀; read the time at which V reaches that value.
walkthrough: Point X is where V = 1.0 V; read down to the time axis: t = 20 s.
After one time constant V = V₀e⁻¹ = 0.37 V₀, so RC = 20 s

graph.alt: Exponential decay of p.d. from 2.7 V towards zero over 60 s, with point X marked where the p.d. has fallen to 1.0 V at 20 s

practice.question: The graph shows how the charge Q on a capacitor varies with time t as it discharges through a resistor in a timing circuit. The tangent to the curve at X, where t = 0, is drawn. Use the graph to determine the initial discharge current in μA.
practice.hint: Current is the rate of change of charge, I = −ΔQ / Δt, so the magnitude of the gradient of the tangent at t = 0 is the initial current; μC per second is μA.
walkthrough: The tangent at X passes through (0 s, 600 μC) and (30 s, 0 μC).

graph.alt: Exponential decay of charge in μC from 600 μC at t = 0, with the tangent at t = 0 drawn from (0, 600 μC) down to (30 s, 0)

practice.question: A 1000 μF capacitor discharges through a resistor. The graph shows ln V plotted against time t, where V is the p.d. across the capacitor, with the best-fit line drawn through A and B. Use the graph to determine the resistance of the resistor in kΩ.
practice.hint: Taking logs of V = V₀e^(−t/RC) gives ln V = ln V₀ − t / RC, so the gradient is −1 / RC; find RC, then divide by C in farads.
walkthrough: ln V = ln V₀ − t / RC, so the gradient of the line is −1 / RC.

graph.alt: Data crosses of ln V against time with a straight best-fit line from A (0, 2.5) to B (100 s, 0.5)
